terms.short: Interest minus income for holding till expiry
terms.definition: What it costs to hold the underlying until the futures expire: interest on the money tied up, minus any dividends the holder receives. It's why index futures usually trade above spot.
examples: With rates at 6% and almost no dividends due, a month's cost of carry on the Nifty is about half a percent.
The client asked why the futures cost more than the shares: buyers pay the cost of carry.
Risk recalculates the cost of carry whenever rates or dividend forecasts change.
terms.fill: Buying the stock today ties up money that could earn interest, less any dividends you'd collect. That net cost of holding it until expiry is the ____.
wrong: Brokerage paid each time you roll a position
Margin blocked for holding a futures position
Tax on futures gains held past expiry

calcs.q: The Nifty is at 20,000, interest rates are 6% a year and no dividends are due. How many points of carry are in the 3-month future?

tf.s: A big dividend due before expiry pushes the futures price up.
tf.why: The futures buyer doesn't get the dividend, so expected dividends are subtracted and the future trades lower.

terms.short: What a future should cost, from spot and carry
terms.definition: The price a futures contract should trade at, given today's spot price, interest rates and expected dividends. If the future drifts far from it, arbitrage pulls it back.
examples: Futures are 40 points over fair value, so the arb desks are selling futures and buying the stocks.
The analyst works out futures fair value from spot, the interest rate and expected dividends.
Risk flags days when the Nifty future strays far from its futures fair value.
terms.fill: Spot plus interest to expiry, minus expected dividends, is the ____.
wrong: Last traded price of the near-month contract
Price the exchange uses for daily margin
Average of the bid and ask on the future

calcs.q: A stock is at 1,000, interest is 6% a year, and a ₹10 dividend is due before the 1-month future expires. What's the future's fair value?

terms.short: Gap between futures and spot price
terms.definition: The gap between a futures price and the spot price. On equity index futures it's usually quoted as futures minus spot, so a positive basis means the future trades at a premium. Commodity hedgers and many textbooks use spot minus futures instead, so check which way round it's quoted.
examples: Nifty basis is 180 points with a month to go, rich against the 120 that carry explains.
The arb desk sells futures when the basis is rich and buys them back near expiry.
The client asked why the futures price was above the Nifty: that gap is the basis.
terms.fill: Nifty futures at 24,150 against spot at 24,000 means a ____ of 150 points.
wrong: One hundredth of a percent
Gap between the bid and the ask
Price paid for an option

calcs.q: Spot is 24,000 and the near-month future is 24,150. What's the basis as a percentage of spot?

tf.s: The basis on index futures shrinks towards zero as expiry nears.

terms.short: Futures above spot, later months higher
terms.definition: When futures trade above the spot price, and longer-dated contracts above nearer ones. It's the normal state for Indian index futures, because the interest cost outweighs dividends.
examples: Crude is in steep contango, so rolling a long position costs money every month.
The client asked why rolling her crude futures kept costing money: the market was in contango.
The commodity analyst expects contango to deepen while stockpiles keep rising.
terms.fill: Near month at 24,100, next month at 24,250 and far month at 24,400: the curve is in ____.
wrong: Futures below spot, later months lower
Futures exactly equal to spot
Spot rising faster than futures

tf.s: In contango, a long futures position that's rolled every month gives up some return to the roll.
tf.why: You sell the cheaper expiring contract and buy the dearer next one, which then drifts down towards spot.

terms.short: Futures below spot, later months lower
terms.definition: When futures trade below the spot price, or longer-dated contracts below nearer ones. It happens when holding the asset pays, such as a big dividend due before expiry, or when the physical good is scarce right now.
examples: The stock future is in backwardation because a large dividend falls before expiry.
The analyst says backwardation in crude points to tight supply right now.
Risk notes that rolling a long future in backwardation earns a small gain each month.
terms.fill: The future trades 15 below spot because a big dividend falls before expiry: the stock is in ____.
wrong: Futures above spot, later months higher
A futures position rolled to the next month
A future that has gone past expiry

tf.s: Futures trading below spot always means there's free arbitrage money.
tf.why: Dividends due before expiry, or a cost to borrow the stock, can justify it.

terms.short: Futures and spot meeting at expiry
terms.definition: The way a futures price closes in on the spot price as expiry approaches, because the carry left shrinks with time. At expiry they meet, since the contract settles at the underlying's closing price.
examples: The basis was 120 points three weeks out and almost nothing on expiry day: convergence at work.
The arb desk holds its spread trade to expiry and lets convergence close the gap to zero.
The client asked why her future and the stock ended at the same price: convergence on expiry day.
terms.fill: As expiry nears, the carry left shrinks and the futures price is pulled to spot. This is called ____.
wrong: Two stocks moving the same way
Futures volume moving to the next month
Option prices falling as expiry nears

tf.s: If the Nifty closes expiry day at 24,210, a near-month future bought at 24,300 loses 90 points per unit.
tf.why: The future settles at the index's closing value, so 24,210 − 24,300 = −90.

terms.short: The futures contract expiring first
terms.definition: The futures contract that expires soonest. NSE lists three monthly index futures at a time, the near, mid and far month, and most of the trading and open interest sits in the near month.
examples: All the liquidity is in the near month, so we only roll in the last week.
The desk trades the near-month contract because the far months barely trade.
Risk prefers hedges in the near-month contract, where the spread is tightest.
terms.fill: On NSE, the soonest-expiring of the three monthly futures is the ____.
wrong: The contract that expires last
A future on next month's index level
An option expiring this week

tf.s: NSE lists three monthly index futures at a time: near, mid and far month.

terms.short: Moving a futures position to the next month
terms.definition: Closing a futures position in the expiring contract and opening the same position in a later month, so the trade carries on past expiry. Desks usually do it in the last week or so before expiry.
examples: We'll do the rollover on Monday, before the spread widens into expiry.
The analyst reads a strong rollover into the next series as a sign traders expect the trend to continue.
The client asked what rollover means: closing this month's future and buying next month's.
terms.fill: Selling your expiring Nifty future and buying next month's to keep the position on is a ____.
wrong: Carrying an intraday trade to the next day
Selling a stock and buying it back the next day
Moving margin from one broker to another

terms.short: Price gap paid to move to the next month
terms.definition: The price difference between the next-month and current-month futures, which a long pays (and a short collects) when rolling. Desks quote it in points or as a percentage; a rich roll hints that longs are keen to stay in.
examples: The Nifty roll is trading at 160 points, a bit above fair carry.
The desk compares the rollover cost with fair carry before deciding when to roll.
Risk tracks rollover cost each month, because an expensive roll eats into the hedge.
terms.fill: Next month trades 180 points over the current month, so moving a long position forward costs 180 points. That gap is the ____.
wrong: Brokerage charged on each futures trade
Gap between futures and spot
Margin needed for the next month

calcs.q: The current-month future is at 24,000 and next month is at 24,180. What's the rollover cost as a percentage?

terms.short: Share of open interest carried to next month
terms.definition: On expiry day, the open interest in the mid and far months as a share of all open interest. High rollovers mean traders are keeping positions on; read it alongside price to tell whether it's longs or shorts staying.
examples: Nifty rollovers came in at 78%, above the three-month average.
The analyst says the high rollover percentage in bank futures shows traders are staying long.
The client asked what a 75% rollover percentage means: three quarters of positions moved to next month.
terms.fill: Of 100 lakh shares of open interest at expiry, 70 lakh sit in the next two months, so the ____ is 70%.
wrong: Share of trades done by algos
Share of options that expire worthless
Share of volume in the near month

calcs.q: At expiry, open interest is 30 lakh in the near month, 60 lakh in the mid month and 10 lakh in the far month. What's the rollover percentage?

terms.short: Buy spot, sell futures, earn the basis
terms.definition: Buying a stock in the cash market and selling its future at the same time, then holding both to expiry. The two prices converge, so the trade locks in the basis, which works like a short-term interest rate.
examples: The cash-futures arb is paying 7% annualised this month, better than a liquid fund.
Risk asked how much margin the cash-and-carry arbitrage book needs on expiry day.
The client asked how her arbitrage fund earns money: it runs cash-and-carry arbitrage on stocks and futures.
terms.fill: Buy the stock at 1,000, sell the month's future at 1,006, hold both to expiry and pocket 6. That's a ____.
wrong: Buying futures and selling the stock
Holding a stock bought with borrowed money
Selling an option and holding cash against it

calcs.q: A stock is at 1,000 and its future, 30 days from expiry, is at 1,005. Before costs, roughly what annualised return does buying the stock and selling the future earn?

tf.s: Once it's on, a cash-and-carry trade earns the same whether the stock rises or falls.
tf.why: Any gain on the stock is lost on the short future, and the other way round; what's left is the basis.

terms.short: Sell spot, buy futures when futures are cheap
terms.definition: Selling a stock you hold and buying its future when the future trades below fair value, then buying the stock back at expiry. Shorting stock beyond the day needs a borrow through SLB, so it's mostly done by funds that already own the shares.
examples: Futures went to a discount, so the fund sold its shares and bought futures to earn the gap.
When futures slipped below spot, the fund ran reverse cash-and-carry: it sold shares and bought futures.
Risk notes that only holders of the shares can run reverse cash-and-carry cheaply, since shorting stock is hard.
terms.fill: The future trades 8 below fair value, so a fund that owns the stock sells it and buys the future instead. That's a ____ trade.
wrong: Buying the stock and selling its future
Rolling a short future to the next month
Buying back shares the company issued

terms.short: Mutual fund that runs cash-futures arbitrage
terms.definition: An Indian mutual fund category that earns mainly by buying stocks and selling their futures. SEBI's rules require at least 65% in equity, but the positions are hedged with futures, so returns look like short-term interest rates rather than stock market returns.
examples: Arbitrage fund returns jump in months when futures premiums are rich.
The client parks short-term money in her arbitrage fund because it's taxed like equity.
Risk notes that arbitrage fund returns dip when futures premiums shrink.
terms.fill: A mutual fund that holds stocks hedged with short futures, and earns close to a money-market rate, is an ____.
wrong: Fund that bets on mergers going through
Fund that invests only in government bonds
Fund that copies an index

tf.s: An arbitrage fund loses heavily when the Nifty falls 10%.
tf.why: Its stocks are hedged with short futures, so market moves largely cancel out.

terms.short: Risk that the hedge and the asset drift apart
terms.definition: The risk that a hedge doesn't move exactly with what it protects, because the futures price and the price you care about drift apart. It shows up when you hedge with a related contract, or close the hedge before expiry.
examples: Hedging a midcap portfolio with Nifty futures leaves a lot of basis risk.
The desk hedged the bank stocks with Bank Nifty futures, accepting some basis risk.
Risk measures the basis risk left after each hedge, not just the exposure hedged.
terms.fill: You must lift a futures hedge two weeks before expiry, when the gap between the future and spot could be anything. That uncertainty is ____.
wrong: Risk that rates rise by one basis point
Risk that the exchange changes the lot size
Risk of losing the whole premium on an option

terms.short: Return from rolling futures each month
terms.definition: The part of a futures position's return that comes from contracts drifting towards spot as they near expiry, picked up each time the position is rolled. It's negative for longs in contango and positive in backwardation.
examples: The commodity fund lost 5% a year to negative roll yield even though spot was flat.
The commodity analyst says roll yield, not spot, drove most of the fund's return.
The client asked why her commodity fund lagged the price of crude: negative roll yield.
terms.fill: Crude spot was flat all year, yet the long futures fund lost money each time it moved into dearer contracts. It had a negative ____.
wrong: Interest earned on margin money
Dividend paid on the underlying stock
Yield on a bond held to maturity

tf.s: A long futures position in a backwardated market tends to earn a positive roll yield.

terms.short: A private deal to trade later at a fixed price
terms.definition: An agreement between two parties to buy or sell something on a future date at a price fixed today. Unlike a futures contract it is private and tailor-made, with no exchange, no daily mark-to-market and no clearing house, so each side takes the risk that the other doesn't pay. Indian importers and exporters hedge the rupee with bank forwards.
examples: The importer booked a three-month forward contract with its bank to lock in the dollar rate.
A forward contract can be for any amount and date; futures come in fixed lots and expiries.
There's no daily margin on the forward contract, but the bank checks our credit line.
terms.fill: A tailor-made deal with a bank to buy dollars in 90 days at a rate fixed today is a ____.
wrong: A standard contract traded on an exchange with daily settlement
The right, but not the duty, to buy at a set price
A loan secured against shares

tf.s: A forward contract is settled through the exchange's clearing corporation every day.
tf.why: That's a futures contract. A forward is private between two parties and usually settles once, on its date.

terms.short: Loan to a borrower that pays interest
terms.definition: A loan you make to a government or company by buying a security from it. The issuer pays interest, called the coupon, on set dates and repays the face value when the bond matures.
examples: The company raised ₹2,000 crore through a five-year bond paying 8%.
The client asked why her bond fell in value when rates rose.
Risk checks each bond the fund holds for its credit rating and when it matures.
terms.fill: A company borrows ₹500 crore from investors for five years, paying 8% a year and returning the money at the end. It has issued a ____.
wrong: A share that makes you part-owner of a company
A contract to buy an asset on a future date
A guarantee a bank gives on a client's loan

tf.s: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall.
tf.why: Their fixed coupons look worse next to new bonds paying more, so their prices drop until the yields match.

terms.short: Interest a bond pays, as % of face value
terms.definition: The interest a bond pays each year, as a percentage of its face value. Indian government bonds pay it in two halves, six months apart. It's fixed when the bond is issued, whatever happens to its price later.
examples: It's a 7.1% bond, so every ₹100 of face value earns ₹3.55 each half-year.
The client wants a bond with a high coupon to pay her monthly bills.
The analyst notes the new bond's coupon is paid twice a year: ₹3.60 each time on ₹100.
terms.fill: A bond pays ₹7 a year on every ₹100 of face value, whatever price it trades at. Its ____ is 7%.
wrong: Return a bond earns if held to maturity at today's price
Discount at which a bond is sold
Fee paid to the bank that arranged the bond

calcs.q: A G-sec with ₹100 face value has a 7.2% coupon, paid half-yearly. How much is each payment per ₹100?
calcs.why: 7.2% × ₹100 = ₹7.20 a year, paid in two halves of ₹3.60.

terms.short: Yearly return if bought now and held to the end
terms.definition: The yearly return a bond gives if you buy it at today's price, collect every coupon and hold it until it's repaid. It's the single rate that makes all those payments add up to the price. When traders say rates rose, they usually mean these went up.
examples: The 10-year is at 6.6%, up 8 bp after the policy.
The client compared the bond's yield to maturity with her FD rate.
Risk notes the bond's yield to maturity assumes every coupon is reinvested at that same rate.
terms.fill: A bond bought below face value pays its coupons and then rises to ₹100 at the end. The annual return from all of that is its ____.
wrong: The interest rate printed on the bond
The bond's price as a percentage of face value
The number of years until the bond is repaid

calcs.q: A one-year bond with no coupon repays ₹100 and costs ₹94. Roughly what's its yield to maturity?

tf.s: A bond trading above face value has a yield to maturity below its coupon.
tf.why: You pay more than ₹100 but only get ₹100 back, and that loss at the end drags the return below the coupon.

terms.short: Coupon built up since the last payment
terms.definition: The part of the next coupon that has built up since the last payment. A buyer pays it to the seller on top of the quoted price, since the buyer will collect the whole coupon. Quoted price plus this is the dirty price.
examples: The clean price is 101.20; with accrued interest the buyer pays 103.10.
The client asked why she paid more than the quoted price: the seller gets the accrued interest.
The bond desk adds accrued interest to the clean price before confirming the trade.
terms.fill: Three months after the last coupon, a buyer pays the quoted price plus the interest built up since then. That extra is the ____.
wrong: Interest that's overdue and unpaid
Interest earned on margin money
A coupon that's been reinvested

calcs.q: A bond with an 8% coupon, paid half-yearly, last paid a coupon 3 months ago. How much interest has built up per ₹100 of face value?

terms.short: % price change for a 1-point move in yield
terms.definition: How sensitive a bond's price is to its yield: roughly the percentage the price falls for each percentage point the yield rises. Long bonds with low coupons have the most; a 10-year government bond is around 7.
examples: With a modified duration of 7, the fund loses about 0.7% if yields rise 10 bp.
Risk caps the fund's modified duration at 4 years before the policy.
The client asked how much her gilt fund could fall: with a modified duration of 8, about 8% if yields rise 1 point.
terms.fill: A bond's price falls about 6% when its yield rises by one percentage point, so its ____ is about 6.
wrong: Years left until the bond is repaid
Number of coupons still to be paid
How long a bond trade takes to settle
terms.formula: % price change ≈ −modified duration × change in yield

calcs.q: A bond fund has a modified duration of 5. Yields rise by 0.40 percentage points. Roughly how much does the fund lose?

tf.s: Other things equal, a longer bond is more sensitive to changes in yield.

aliases: price value of a basis point
terms.short: Rupee change in value for a 1 bp yield move
terms.definition: How much a bond position gains or loses, in rupees, when yields move by one basis point. Rates desks size and limit their risk with it.
examples: Our book's PV01 is ₹4 lakh, so a 10 bp sell-off costs ₹40 lakh.
Risk sets each trader's limit in PV01, so position sizes adjust to bond maturity.
The desk cut its PV01 before the inflation data.
terms.fill: The rates desk loses ₹2 lakh for every 1 bp rise in yields. That ₹2 lakh is its ____.
wrong: Price of a bond with ₹1 of face value
Yield on the shortest government bond
Interest a bond pays each day

calcs.q: You hold ₹100 crore of bonds with a modified duration of 6. Roughly what's the PV01?

terms.short: How a bond's duration shifts as yields move
terms.definition: The curve in a bond's price–yield line. Duration isn't constant, so prices rise more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount. Ordinary bonds have positive convexity, which helps the holder in big moves.
examples: In a 100 bp rally, convexity adds about half a point on top of what duration predicts.
The analyst likes the long bond's convexity: it gains more when yields fall than it loses when they rise.
Risk adds convexity to the duration estimate for big rate moves.
terms.fill: Yields fell 1 point and the bond gained 7.6%; when they rose 1 point it lost only 6.8%. The gap comes from ____.
wrong: Extra yield a company bond pays over government bonds
Years until a bond is repaid
Gap between short and long-term yields

terms.short: Yields plotted from short to long maturities
terms.definition: A line joining the yields of government bonds from the shortest maturity to the longest. It usually slopes up, since lenders want more for tying money up longer; when short yields rise above long ones it's inverted, which often comes before a slowdown.
examples: The curve steepened as the 10-year sold off while T-bills held steady.
The economist says the yield curve is flattening as markets price in more hikes.
The client asked why long bonds pay more than short ones: the yield curve usually slopes up.
terms.fill: Plot the yields of 1-year, 5-year, 10-year and 30-year government bonds and join the dots. That line is the ____.
wrong: Chart of one bond's price over time
Line showing how inflation changes over a year
Gap between government and company bond yields

tf.s: An inverted yield curve means short-term government bonds yield more than long-term ones.

terms.short: Extra yield over a government bond
terms.definition: The extra yield a company bond pays over a government bond of the same maturity, to make up for the risk that the company doesn't pay. It widens when investors get nervous and narrows when they're relaxed.
examples: AAA spreads are 70 bp over G-secs; lower-rated paper is far wider.
Risk's stress test widens every credit spread by 200 bp.
The client asked why the NBFC bond pays 3% more than a G-sec: that's the credit spread for its risk.
terms.fill: A 5-year AAA company bond yields 7.4% while the 5-year G-sec yields 6.7%. The 70 bp gap is the ____.
wrong: Gap between a bond's bid and ask prices
Gap between the coupon and the yield
Fee a bank charges to arrange a bond

calcs.q: A company bond yields 8.10% and a government bond of the same maturity yields 6.85%. What's the credit spread?

terms.short: Pays no coupons, sold below face value
terms.definition: A bond that pays no interest along the way. It is bought at a discount and repaid at face value on maturity; the gap is the return. Treasury bills are zero-coupon. Because all the cash comes at the end, its duration equals its maturity, so its price is more sensitive to rates than a coupon bond of the same maturity.
examples: The 364-day T-bill is a zero-coupon bond: buy at ₹93.50, get ₹100 back.
A ten-year zero-coupon bond swings far more with rates than a ten-year coupon bond.
Strips turn each coupon of a G-sec into its own zero-coupon bond.
terms.fill: A bond bought at ₹93 that pays nothing until it repays ₹100 at maturity is a ____.
wrong: A bond that pays a floating coupon
A bond with no fixed maturity date
A bond the issuer can repay early

calcs.q: A one-year zero-coupon bond repays ₹100. If its yield is 7%, what is its price?
calcs.why: 100 ÷ 1.07 ≈ ₹93.46. Note it's not 100 − 7: the discount earns 7% on the price paid.

terms.short: Weighted average time to a bond's cash flows
terms.definition: The average time until a bond's cash flows arrive, each weighted by its share of the bond's present value, in years. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration is its maturity; coupons pull it shorter. Divide it by (1 + yield) to get modified duration, the price sensitivity to rates.
examples: The ten-year G-sec has a Macaulay duration of about seven years, because of its coupons.
For a zero-coupon bond, Macaulay duration equals maturity.
Divide Macaulay duration by 1 plus the yield to get the modified duration.
terms.fill: The present-value-weighted average time until a bond's cash flows arrive is its ____.
wrong: The time left until the bond matures
The percentage price change for a 1% rate move
The rupee change for a one basis point move

calcs.q: A bond has a Macaulay duration of 5 years and an annual yield of 8%. What is its modified duration?
calcs.why: 5 ÷ 1.08 ≈ 4.63, so a 1% rise in yield cuts the price by about 4.6%.

terms.short: Bond price without and with accrued interest
terms.definition: A bond's clean price leaves out the interest that has built up since the last coupon; the dirty price (also called the full or invoice price) includes it. Indian G-secs are quoted clean, but the buyer pays the dirty price on settlement, because the seller has earned the interest so far.
examples: The G-sec is quoted at ₹101.20 clean, but we'll pay ₹102.85 dirty with accrued interest.
Quoting clean stops the price jumping every coupon date.
The dirty price drops on the coupon date; the clean price doesn't.
terms.fill: Quoted price plus the interest built up since the last coupon gives the ____.
wrong: The price after a bond's credit rating is cut
Bid and offer prices from two dealers
The price before and after the issuer's results
terms.formula: Dirty price = Clean price + Accrued interest

calcs.q: A bond's clean price is ₹100.00 and accrued interest is ₹1.50. What does the buyer pay?

terms.short: Swap fixed-rate payments for floating ones
terms.definition: An agreement to exchange interest payments on a notional amount: one side pays a fixed rate, the other a floating rate, and only the difference changes hands. No principal is exchanged. Banks and companies use swaps to turn floating-rate loans into fixed or the other way round. In India the main one is the overnight indexed swap on MIBOR.
examples: The company paid fixed on a five-year interest rate swap to lock in its loan cost.
The bank received fixed in the swap, betting rates would fall.
Swap rates moved before bonds did after the RBI policy.
terms.fill: Paying 6.5% fixed and receiving a floating rate on ₹100 crore notional is an ____.
wrong: A loan swapped from one bank to another
Exchanging one bond for another of the same issuer
Insurance against a borrower defaulting

tf.s: In an interest rate swap the two sides exchange the full notional at the start and the end.
tf.why: Only the interest payments are exchanged, usually netted. The notional just sizes them; it never changes hands.
